title: Bring your Fabric data into your next app with connectors
author: mk_sunitha

content.text:
Most business applications start with data that already exists. Customer orders may live in a Fabric SQL database. Inventory history may be in a Lakehouse. Sales performance may already be modeled in Power BI. The opportunity is not to move that data again, but to turn trusted data into an experience that helps people make decisions and take action.
Connectors in Fabric Apps shorten that path. They give an app a consistent way to work with Fabric data, so developers can spend less time on integration plumbing and more time building the experience users need.
Connect to the Fabric data you already trust. Build the experience your users need. Keep the application close to the data and governance foundation already in place.
Instead of beginning with infrastructure, start with the customer's need: What should this app help someone understand, decide, or do?
From data to an application
Imagine a large telecommunications provider operating thousands of cell sites and serving millions of customers. Network telemetry may stream into a Lakehouse; service-impact and incident data may live in a Fabric SQL database; and trusted availability and capacity measures may already be modeled in Power BI.
A report can show where the service is degrading. But a network operations engineer may need to go further:
• Which sites and customers are affected?
• Is the issue driven by congestion, equipment, power, or an upstream dependency?
• What maintenance work or recent changes are associated with the site?
• Can I create or update an incident and route the next action from the same experience?
This is where a Fabric App adds value. Connectors let the app combine governed network and operational data in one task-oriented experience for investigation, triage, and action.
Architecture: Network operations app
Figure: Fabric data remains the foundation; connectors bring network and operational context into a task-oriented Fabric App.
Network telemetry remains in Fabric; operational records stay in their governed source; and trusted measures continue to come from the semantic model. The Fabric App brings those sources together so an engineer can move from a network signal to an informed operational action without reconstructing context across multiple tools.
Choose the connector that matches the job
Choose the connector that matches the Fabric item and the job the app needs to perform. Fabric Apps supports documented connector patterns for lakehouse SQL analytics endpoints, warehouses, SQL databases in Fabric, and Power BI semantic models.
Fabric source
Connector type
Documented operations
Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint
fabric-sqlanalytics
Read
Warehouse
fabric-warehouse
Read, create, update, delete
SQL database in Fabric
fabric-sqldatabase
Read, create, update, delete
Power BI semantic model
fabric-semanticmodel
executeQuery
Request only the operations the scenario needs. For example, a read-only inventory experience should not request write access. An operational app that updates a warehouse or SQL database should make that requirement explicit.
Three real-world patterns
Incident triage
A telecommunications provider can build a network operations app on a Lakehouse, Fabric SQL database, and semantic model. An engineer can search for a cell site; review latency, congestion, availability, and impacted services; inspect recent maintenance or configuration changes; and create or update the operational incident from one experience.
Value: The engineer moves from detecting service degradation to understanding impact and coordinating the next action without switching across disconnected monitoring and case-management views.
Customer 360 for sellers
A sales team may have accounts and order data in a warehouse, product signals in a Lakehouse, and trusted revenue measures in a semantic model. A Fabric App can organize this information around the account and add a tailored experience for exploration, notes, recommended next steps, or AI-assisted questions.
Value: The app is designed around the seller’s job, not around the boundaries between data systems.
Retail store operations from a semantic model
Imagine a retailer such as Nordstrom with trusted sales, inventory, fulfillment, and customer-service measures already defined in a Power BI semantic model. A Fabric App can use that model as the analytical foundation for a store operations experience where a manager reviews daily performance, identifies products at risk of stocking out, investigates order or pickup delays, and coordinates the next action with the store team.
Value: Store teams reuse trusted business measures and move from insight to action without recreating logic or switching across multiple reports and operational tools.
Start with one focused workflow
A good first app starts with a narrow, valuable job. The builder journey is:
• Create or initialize a Fabric Apps project.
• Identify the Fabric item behind the workflow.
• Add a connector with only the operations the app needs.
• Test with the permissions and data boundaries expected for users.
For example, a read-only warehouse connection can expose governed site and service-impact data to the app:
npx rayfin connector add \
--type fabric-warehouse \
--workspace-id YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID \
--item-id YOUR_WAREHOUSE_ITEM_ID \
--name network-operations \
--operations read
The connector is added to the project configuration and can then be used through the generated connector interface. For complete syntax, supported operations, prerequisites, and current limitations, see Connect Fabric Apps to Fabric data.
Build from the data you already trust
Your most valuable business data is already in Microsoft Fabric. Connectors help you turn that data into focused applications that do more than display insight by helping you complete real business tasks. Get started with Fabric App and connect to your data.
